input.said: What does Seth say about Chalmers' neural replacement thought experiment?

cases.reply:
Seth argues the thought experiment fails at the start, because its central premise can't be met. The experiment asks us to imagine swapping brain parts one by one for silicon parts that work in exactly the same way. It is used to conclude that consciousness doesn't depend on what the brain is made of. Seth says the argument "fails at its first hurdle", since no part of the brain can be replaced by a perfect silicon equivalent [spya-ahtr6e]. He also notes that Hinton recently leaned on the same argument to claim conscious AI is already here [spya-ahtr6e].

His reason for the impossibility comes just before this. Brain activity is woven together across many scales, which he calls "generative entrenchment". So you can't assume a single neuron could be swapped for a silicon one with its input-output behavior perfectly preserved [spya-jnwfxp]. His example is work by Chintaluri and Vogels. They found that some neurons fire to clear metabolic waste, so a perfect replacement would need its own silicon metabolism, which silicon isn't suited to [spya-un9fjn].

In the larger argument, this belongs to the first of his four arguments, "Brains Are Not Computers". It supports his point that you can't cleanly separate what a brain does from what it is. That in turn undermines computational functionalism, the view that the right computation is enough for consciousness [spya-p4vmm0].

My inference is that the objection targets the thought experiment's premise (perfect functional replacement) and not its logic. If the replacement parts really could be perfect, Seth's reply wouldn't apply. The article doesn't discuss that case or how Chalmers himself would respond.
